newsitem.title: USA: Tudjman in U.S. for cancer treatment-U.S. officials.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman in U.S. for cancer treatment-U.S. officials.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman is seriously ill with stomach cancer and is undergoing treatment at a Washington hospital, U.S. officials said on Friday.

"I can confirm that President Tudjman is at Walter Reed (Army) Hospital," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing. "He is there, obviously, on a visit concerning his health. I am not in a position to talk to you about the status of his health."

The Croatian embassy confirmed Tudjman was at the hospital. It released a statement by his personal physicians saying he was suffering from "digestive problems" and had "a stomach ulcer and enlarged abdominal lymph nodes."

It made no reference to cancer but said Tudjman was "undergoing follow-up medical examinations." It added: "The president feels well and continues to perform his duties and is returning to Croatia by the end of next week."
Meanwhile, Croatian state television on Friday played down reports that Tudjman was seriously ill.
The 74-year-old Croatian president played a prominent role in the collapse of the former Yugoslavia and negotiation of peace in Bosnia last year.
Burns said he arrived at the hospital "quite recently -- just in the last 24 hours or so" but did not know how long Tudjman would stay.
Other U.S. officials said he would be at Walter Reed, one of the top U.S. military hospitals, for a two-week cancer treatment and was then expected to return home.
But U.S. sources said they understood his prognosis was not good, with some officials telling Reuters they had been told he was diagnosed as having less than one year to live.
"I understand that he has cancer of the stomach and that he is very very ill," one official said.
A spokesman for Walter Reed said its policy was not to comment on diplomats being treated there.

The Croatian state-run news agency HINA reported on Wednesday in Zagreb that Tudjman had taken a short break for a "regular medical check-up." A spokesman for his office in Zagreb declined to say how long the break would be.

Along with Serb President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, Tudjman played a key role in the U.S.-led negotiations in Dayton, Ohio, last year that secured an agreement ending nearly four years of war in Bosnia.

Born on May 14, 1922, near Zagreb, Tudjman fought with late Yugoslav leader Josip Broz Tito's partisans against German occupation and its puppet Croatian fascist regime in the Second World War. He became disillusioned with Serb-dominated Yugoslav communism in the 1950s and left the army as a major general in 1961 and obtained a doctorate in history.

Turning to Croatian nationalism, he was jailed twice in the 1970s and early 1980s for "counter-revolution." But he re-emerged to found the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), which pursued Croatian self-rule as Yugoslavia's multinational federation unravelled after Tito's death.

The HDZ ousted the Communists from power in Croatia in 1990, its first free vote since the 1930s. In June 1991, Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia and minority Serbs rebelled with Yugoslav army backing, seizing 30 percent of Croatia in a six-month war halted by a U.N. ceasefire.
Tudjman created a multi-party democracy and launched the conversion of the economy from Yugoslav socialism to Croatian capitalism dedicated to membership of the European Union.
